metadata.narrative: Compose a concise technical report sketching an experimental plan for deciding whether a modern vision-language model could stand in for human specialists when labeling medical images of skin lesions.
metadata.run_desc: aus_agent research harness (bedrock/au.anthropic.claude-sonnet-5): iterative hybrid dense+sparse ClimbMix search + document fetch, strict-JSON cited sentence answers.

answer.text: This report sketches an experimental plan to test whether a modern vision-language model (VLM) could substitute for human dermatology specialists in labeling skin lesion images, drawing on prior AI-vs-clinician dermatology studies.
Background: dermatologist shortages motivate VLM systems like SkinGPT, SkinGPT-4 and MedDr, fine-tuned on dermatology image-text data to produce diagnoses.
Med-Flamingo shows multimodal few-shot prompting can yield clinician-preferred medical VQA answers, a template for prompting a VLM on lesion labeling.
Stanford's Esteva et al. trained a CNN on ~129,450 images that matched 21 board-certified dermatologists on biopsy-confirmed classification, the classic comparison design to emulate.
A Lancet Oncology study with 511 readers across 63 countries found deep learning outperforming human experts on dermatoscopic classification, showing the value of large multi-country reader panels.
Google's differential-diagnosis AI (71–91% accuracy) exceeded general/nurse practitioners but underperformed on rare skin tones and melanoma due to data scarcity, motivating subgroup evaluation.
Objective 1: test whether VLM labels agree with, and match the accuracy of, a defined reference standard (ideally histopathology-confirmed) and specialist consensus.

Ground truth should follow the BMJ pathologist-reliability study's approach of a three-expert consensus panel, since even pathologist accuracy against consensus fell to 25–43% for intermediate-difficulty lesions versus 72–92% for clear cases.
Real biopsy-confirmed images matter: the Youzhi AI system showed significantly lower real-world accuracy than lab-benchmark accuracy despite being comparable to average dermatologists.
The plan should thus use two arms: (a) retrospective benchmarking on curated sets like the ISIC archive/HAM10000, and (b) a prospective real-world clinical arm.
Report full confusion-matrix metrics (sensitivity, specificity, PPV/NPV, F-measure), not just accuracy, per prior AI-vs-dermatologist comparisons.
Use paired statistical tests—McNemar's test and AUC equivalence/non-inferiority comparisons—since the goal is establishing the VLM is not unacceptably worse, not necessarily superior.
Pre-specify a clinically acceptable non-inferiority margin rather than a simple superiority test.
FDA statistical guidance flags low disease prevalence, scarce truth data, calibration, and multi-class design as key challenges for evaluating AI devices, all relevant to multi-class lesion labeling.
Objective 2: test actual visual grounding, since adding images to ChatGPT-4V did not improve—and reduced top-1—diagnostic accuracy versus text-only across 363 case reports.
Use feature-conditioning probes (holding ABCDE features constant, altering pigmentation/annotations) as done for GPT-4V and LLaVA on melanoma-vs-nevus discrimination.
That study found GPT-4V reached 85% accuracy versus 45% for LLaVA, but both showed color bias and LLaVA failed on skin of color, motivating skin-tone-stratified test sets.
Adopt structured human-rater protocols (Likert ratings of interpretation correctness, advice correctness/danger, trainee-learning suitability) as used to evaluate GPT-4V dermatologic outputs.
Include retrieval- and chain-of-thought-augmented pipelines as an experimental arm, since such GPT-4V pipelines retrieved correct skin conditions 85% of the time from images plus brief history.

Objective 3: assess human-AI teaming, since dermatologist confidence rose when an AI classifier agreed (even if wrong) and fell when it disagreed, with only nonsignificant accuracy gains after one practice session.

A South Korean RCT found real-time CNN assistance significantly helped non-dermatology trainees (30.7%→54.7%) but not residents, and caused a 12.2% accuracy drop when top-3 AI predictions were all wrong.
Stratify analysis by rater experience level and assisted-vs-unassisted condition, replicating this RCT design.
Objective 4 (fairness): test across Fitzpatrick types, since Black skin comprises only 5–10% of some dermatology databases, risking high aggregate but poor subgroup accuracy.
Use a Statistical Parity Difference-based fairness score across skin-tone subgroups alongside accuracy and latency.
Audit datasets with multidimensional skin-color measures beyond Fitzpatrick, which misses hue variation (e.g., dark-yellow undertones).
Objective 5 (safety): catalog hallucination risk, since multimodal LLMs can fabricate non-existent visual features, which could yield fabricated lesion characteristics.
Follow FUTURE-AI guidance: justify need for explainability, validate explanations with end users, and require calibrated confidence outputs.
Use Grad-CAM-style attribution maps to compare VLM attention against dermatologists' documented eye-movement patterns during examination.
Frame deployment scenarios against existing cleared devices like DermaSensor (cleared as a triage aid for already-flagged lesions, not standalone screening).
Contrast with IDx-DR, the first FDA-authorized autonomous diagnostic AI (diabetic retinopathy, no specialist review required), as the regulatory bar for true replacement versus assistance.

Proposed pipeline: (1) assemble a stratified, pathology-confirmed test set across ISIC/HAM10000 classes and skin-tone subgroups; (2) define reference diagnosis via expert consensus; (3) run the VLM under multiple prompting strategies versus individual specialists and consensus.

(4) Compute accuracy/sensitivity/specificity/AUC/calibration with paired non-inferiority tests; (5) run a teaming sub-study on confidence and switching behavior; (6) ablate image input to quantify visual reliance.
(7) Add a prospective real-world arm to capture lab-to-clinic performance gaps; (8) report fairness and explainability/uncertainty metrics alongside aggregate performance.

Limitations: small comparator panels limit generalizability, unmasked designs risk bias, and human inter-rater variability means VLMs must be judged against a distribution of expert opinion, not one 'true' standard.

Overall, evidence suggests VLMs can approach human accuracy on narrow melanoma/nevus tasks but show inconsistent visual grounding, bias susceptibility, and uneven benefit by user expertise, favoring a non-inferiority/augmentation framing over outright replacement.
